The most expensive line in your AI budget is the judgement you didn't hire.

Most boards are being shown AI-enabled supply chain savings this year. Very few of those numbers survive a second question.

A global coffee chain now counts inventory with cameras. The app mislabels the milk. Four CEOs in five years have blamed empty shelves for lost sales. The software worked — the network beneath it could not be modelled cleanly.

A footwear brand's planning system ordered too much of the slow sellers and too little of the bestsellers: $100 million in lost sales, 20% off the share price in a day. The algorithm wasn't the failure. No one ever met to review the forecast.

And better data doesn't rescue you. A study of 4,523 grocery products found sharper forecasts cut inventory while making ordering up to 31% more erratic. The model had no view of which trade-off the business wanted.

Same gap every time. Not modelling. Judgement.

Closing it is not a hiring-volume problem. It is a rare-profile problem. Most operators spend their careers inside the systems they inherited. Most AI people have never owned a service level, a detention charge or a cold-chain excursion. The few who can read the P&L and interrogate the model at the same time will be the ones global supply chains are built around this decade. Where an organisation has one, the advantage compounds. Where it doesn't, it keeps buying models and calling it transformation.

As a global supply chain director owning the whole chain, not a function: ports, CFS, yards, FTWZ, warehousing, 3PL/4PL, contract logistics, cold chain, rail, express, freight forwarding. One AI layer above those core systems so they plan from the same numbers. Above it, a quantum layer held honestly — hybrid today, classical still winning; the formulation is the moat, not the hardware.

That is where I work: domain on one side, AI on the other, and the number in between with my name on it. It is the least comfortable place to stand in this industry, and the most useful.

The scarce hire isn't the person who can buy the model. It's the one who can overrule it.

If you're approving AI supply chain savings nobody in the room can stress-test, that exposure is already on your P&L. It just hasn't been booked yet.

I'd rather argue about this than post about it.

WHY ARE THE COMPANIES REHIRING LAID-OFF EMPLOYEES AS CONTRACTORS?

If AI can replace software engineers, why do companies still need them after layoffs?

The tech industry is going through a major shift.

Companies are investing billions in AI.
Executives are talking about automation.
Software engineers are being told that AI can write code faster, improve productivity, and reduce the need for developers.

But here's the interesting part.

Google has reportedly rehired #6000 #former #employees as contractors after layoffs.

And this raises an important question.

If companies no longer need these people, why bring them back?

The answer may be more complicated than simply saying AI is replacing developers.

When an experienced engineer leaves, a company can lose much more than coding capacity.

It can lose years of institutional knowledge, familiarity with complex systems, architectural decisions, undocumented business logic, and experience handling production incidents.

AI can generate code.

But understanding why a legacy system behaves a certain way, making critical architectural decisions, and taking responsibility for production systems are different challenges.

And this is where the contradiction begins.

A company may reduce its permanent workforce but still need the same expertise to complete projects, maintain systems, or support business operations.

Hiring contractors can offer flexibility without the same long-term employment commitments.

However, this does not mean every layoff is caused by AI, or that every former employee is rehired as a contractor.

The bigger question is whether AI is replacing software engineers or changing how companies choose to employ them.

Because these are two very different things.

If a company eliminates permanent positions but later pays contractors to perform similar work, has it actually eliminated the need for those skills?

Or has it simply changed the employment model?

My perspective is simple:

AI may reduce the time required to write code, but it doesn't automatically eliminate the need for engineering judgment, system knowledge, and accountability.

The companies that understand this distinction will make better long-term decisions about their engineering teams.

What's your take?

Are companies genuinely replacing software engineers with AI, or are some simply shifting from full-time employees to contract-based talent?

As engineering leaders, we are under immense pressure to show the ROI of our AI investments. The developers are happy, the managers are reporting localized speed, but the bottom-line delivery remains stubbornly the same.

The reality is that local efficiency is not system throughput.

If we accelerate code generation but still review, test, and deploy that code using legacy workflows, we haven’t made engineering cheaper—we’ve just built a massive queue of unchecked code waiting for our downstream bottleneck. We have electrified the factory but kept the 19th-century assembly line.

To turn AI capability into actual, verified business value, we need to treat it as a system-wide re-engineering problem, not an isolated coding task:

Pivot to Verified Delivery Economics: Stop measuring activity. No one cares about lines of code generated or seat adoption. Our North Star must be Cost per Verified Production Delivery. A delivery isn't "done" when the code is written—it’s done when it satisfies a strict outcome contract of testing, security, and schema validation, and is safely running in production.

Map the Total Value Stream: If a developer uses AI to cut implementation from six hours to two, but the change sits in review for 18 hours and waits another day for a release window, the cycle time has barely budged. We must track active effort, queue times, and rework across the entire workflow to find out where our bottleneck has migrated.

Tackle "Verification Debt": A massive surge of generated code can quickly bankrupt our testing and review capacity. This is especially dangerous in data engineering, where a pipeline can execute successfully with green checks while generating entirely incorrect business logic. Verification cannot be an afterthought; it must be a first-class, highly automated capability.

Ruthlessly Connect Capacity to Financial Value: Theoretical "hours saved" do not equal cash in the bank. As leaders , we must prove how AI-freed capacity converts into tangible outcomes—whether that's absorbing increased demand without hiring, reducing contractor dependency, or shrinking time-to-market on major revenue drivers.

The next competitive advantage won't belong to the team with the most AI tools. It will belong to the organization that redesigns its entire delivery system to absorb them safely.

AI has made writing code cheaper. It is our job to make the outcomes valuable.

The AI Résumé Trap: 10 Interview Mistakes That Can Cost You the Job

AI can help tailor your résumé, optimize keywords, and improve your professional presentation. But a polished résumé cannot answer interview questions for you. In today's competitive job market, experience alone is not enough. You must demonstrate credibility, results, adaptability, and professionalism.

10 mistakes to avoid:
1. Relying on AI instead of real expertise. Never list skills, certifications, or accomplishments you cannot explain or substantiate.
2. Describing responsibilities instead of results. Explain what you accomplished, how you contributed, and the business value delivered. Use measurable results when possible.
3. Displaying arrogance or overconfidence. Seniority does not excuse interrupting, dismissing questions, or speaking negatively about former colleagues. Demonstrate expertise with humility.
4. Failing to research the employer. Understand the company's business, industry challenges, priorities, and the specific role before the interview.
5. Letting the interviewer control the entire conversation. Answer questions directly, share relevant examples, communicate your value, and ask thoughtful questions. An interview is a two-way conversation.
6. Focusing only on past salary. Research market compensation and consider responsibilities, benefits, flexibility, and career opportunities. Discuss the value you bring.
7. Waiting until the final offer to demonstrate your value. Connect your experience to the employer's needs throughout the hiring process. Clarify expectations and show how you can contribute.
8. Accepting an offer without understanding its terms. Review compensation, benefits, contract duration, schedule, travel, responsibilities, and termination provisions. Make an informed decision that reflects your circumstances.
9. Asking for feedback too late. During the interview, invite questions about any concerns regarding your qualifications. Learn from every interview, even when feedback is unavailable.
10. Pressuring recruiters when qualified candidates are abundant. Repeated demands, ultimatums, and impatient follow-ups can damage your candidacy. Ask about timelines, follow up professionally, and communicate genuine competing-offer deadlines honestly.
The Bottom Line
Your résumé opens the door, but you must prove your value.
Use AI as a tool, not a substitute for experience, judgment, or authenticity. Prepare specific examples, demonstrate results, research the employer, negotiate thoughtfully, and treat everyone with respect.
For displaced professionals, especially in Oil & Gas, career transitions require persistence and adaptability. Your experience still matters. Show employers how it translates into value today.
Confidence gets attention. Credibility, preparation, and professionalism help win the opportunity.
